This analysis relied on observations collected at 1,200 monitoring wells in and around Alameda that are part of the California State Water Resources Control Board’s (SWRCBs) Groundwater Ambient Monitoring and Assessment Program, using observational data available through SWRCB’s GeoTracker 18. 993 wells (out of 1,200) were observed to have a higher groundwater table after the 2022-23 storm season than observed between 2000 and 2020. The highest annual groundwater table shown on Figure 4-13 is based on well observations between 2000 and 2020 (i.e., does not account for the 2022-23 storm season). This would require an updated groundwater analysis to capture well observations post 2020 for the City of Alameda. 207 wells (out of 1,200) were observed to have a lower groundwater table after the 2022-23 storm season than observed between 2000 and 2020. Groundwater table elevations can vary significantly depending on soil characteristics and geology, impervious verses pervious ground surfaces, groundwater flow rates, groundwater pumping, and other factors. An in-depth comparison of groundwater table elevation is also limited by the number of well observations collected each year. Most wells are monitored twice per year, at the end of the summer or early fall when the groundwater table is generally at its lowest, and late spring or early summer when the groundwater table is generally at its highest (if significant rain occurred over the previous winter).
